title: The Fall of Jamshid
text:
Jamshid was one of the greatest kings in Ferdowsi's Shahnameh. Blessed with the divine glory, the farr, he ruled for centuries over a golden age. He taught people to forge weapons and armor, to spin and weave, to build with brick, to work gems and make perfumes and medicines. He organized society into its classes. The demons served him, and he had them raise him on a jeweled throne into the sky. The day he rose up was celebrated as the first Nowruz, the new year.

Under him, the poem says, there was no death or disease, and the world was at peace. But as the years passed, Jamshid came to see all of it as his own work. He gathered the nobles and priests and told them that he alone had brought all this into being, that he knew no king in the world but himself, and that they should call him the creator of the world.

The nobles bowed their heads in silence. At that moment the divine glory left him. His nobles began to drift away, and in time his army deserted him for Zahhak, the usurper from the west. Jamshid fled and hid for a hundred years before Zahhak found him and had him sawn in two.
lesson: Success built with many hands and some luck is easy to start calling your own. The moment you claim all the credit is often the moment people stop following you.
source: Ferdowsi, Shahnameh, the reign of Jamshid
